prompt.context: Your client is a global mining company with a location in South Africa. This particular location is performing below average financially. McKinsey has been hired to identify the problem and make recommendations to address it.
prompt.question: What would you do first to approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: Where is the plant located relative to the port?
clarifying_info.a: The processing plant is located 160 miles inland. It uses a fleet of large trucks to transport minerals from the plant (which is near the mineral source) to a port city. The minerals are then loaded onto barges and shipped to clients around the world.

clarifying_info.q: Does the plant need to operate at full capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the plant needs to operate at maximum capacity to meet customer demand.

clarifying_info.q: What type of minerals does the plant produce?
clarifying_info.a: The minerals produced are commodities with low margins.

exhibits.title: Mighty Mining Trip Time Distribution
exhibits.shows: A histogram showing the distribution of total round trip times (hours) for trucks traveling from the plant to the port and back. The x-axis represents total round trip time in hours (up to 24) and the y-axis shows number of trips (up to 1000).

data.key_feature: Bimodal distribution — one peak in the expected range and a second unexpected peak further right

framework: Revenues: Explore historical data, trends, and product-specific data; benchmark against competitors and other corporate locations

Operations: Assess whether the plant operates at full capacity; identify interruptions (power outages, local protests, theft, unrest); evaluate employee skill level and morale; flag locally specific operational risks in South Africa
Costs (overview): Separate fixed costs (PP&E, overhead) from variable costs (materials, labor, logistics)
COGS detail: Labor, Materials, Shipping/Logistics (transportation is a large portion of product cost for a commodity and should be broken out separately)
Operating Expenses: Administrative, overhead, depreciation & amortization
Transportation (focal area): Because the product is a commodity with thin margins, transportation costs are a disproportionately large share of COGS and warrant deep analysis

questions.prompt: Transportation costs are significantly higher as a portion of COGS than at any other African plant location. Why might this be?
questions.guidance: Look for a range of out-of-the-box ideas covering route efficiency, driver behavior, and security issues. Strong answers include: trucks leaving the plant not fully loaded (increasing number of trips required); poor route planning or drivers not going directly to the port; drivers sleeping on the job or taking excessive breaks; trucks being hijacked along the 160-mile route; drivers paying bribes at road checkpoints.

questions.prompt: You collect historical data on the average time it takes a truck to make the round trip from the plant to the port. What should the distribution graph look like, and what does the actual data reveal?
questions.guidance: Expected shape: a normal distribution centered around the average round-trip time. The actual exhibit shows a bimodal distribution — one peak is consistent with the expected normal distribution, but a second peak appears at a longer time. The candidate should identify the second peak as anomalous and brainstorm causes: certain drivers consistently taking too many breaks, traffic patterns at specific times of day, drivers waiting for bribes at checkpoints, or trucks being delayed by security incidents.

questions.prompt: You discover that the port closes at 10pm and any truck that does not arrive by 10pm must wait until the port opens again at 4am. The minimum round-trip travel time is 7 hours and the plant owns 20 trucks; a barge needs 30 truckloads to reach capacity and ship out. What would you recommend Mighty Mining do about this situation? (The plant must operate at max capacity.)
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify multiple bottlenecks: (1) port hours of operation create a hard deadline, (2) minimum 7-hour round trip constrains when trucks can depart, (3) 20 trucks vs. 30 truckloads needed per barge creates a capacity gap. Rather than just optimizing a number, a strong answer identifies all three constraints and proposes tiered short- and long-term solutions. See recommendation section for full list.

math.setup: Port closes 10pm; opens 4am. Minimum round trip = 7 hours. Therefore latest departure time to make 10pm cutoff = 10pm − 7h = 3pm. Plant owns 20 trucks; barge needs 30 truckloads. Gap = 30 − 20 = 10 additional truckloads needed per barge cycle.
steps: Latest truck departure to meet 10pm port closure: 10:00pm − 7 hours = 3:00pm
Trucks that miss 10pm cutoff must wait 6 hours (10pm to 4am) before unloading, adding 6 wasted hours per delayed trip
With 20 trucks and 30 truckloads needed, at least 2 full rotations (or partial overlap of rotations) are required per barge; any delay reduces effective daily throughput
math.answer: Key insight: every truck delayed past the 10pm cutoff loses ~6 hours of productive time, materially reducing daily throughput. With only 20 trucks vs. 30 needed per barge, the company is already constrained on capacity — port delays compound the problem.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential reasons transportation costs at this plant are significantly higher as a share of COGS than at other African locations?

categories.name: Loading & capacity utilization
ideas: Trucks leaving the plant not fully loaded, increasing total trips required
No consolidation schedule to batch loads

categories.name: Route & driver efficiency
ideas: Drivers not taking the most direct route to the port
Drivers taking excessive rest stops or sleeping on the job
Poor shift scheduling leading to underutilized driving hours

categories.name: Security & local conditions
ideas: Trucks being hijacked along the 160-mile route
Drivers forced to pay bribes at road checkpoints
Local unrest or protests blocking roads and causing delays

categories.name: Fleet & maintenance
ideas: Aging fleet with higher fuel consumption and breakdown frequency
Insufficient truck size relative to available capacity
High maintenance costs increasing per-trip cost

recommendation: In the short term, identify the latest departure time for trucks to reach the port by 10pm and use driver incentives to minimize rest stops and meet the cutoff; restructure driver shifts to maximize loads delivered per day
In the long term, lobby for or negotiate 24-hour port operations, which would benefit all shipping parties and eliminate the cutoff constraint
Evaluate the cost of building a storage facility near the port to hold overnight deliveries vs. the cost of purchasing additional trucks
Analyze upgrading the fleet to larger-capacity trucks to reduce total trips required per barge cycle
Consider leasing trucks vs. purchasing to reduce capital requirements given the plant's already poor financial performance
risks: Since the location is already underperforming, the cost of capital is a critical factor — any capital investment must be evaluated against the NPV of continuing operations or shifting volume to better-performing plants
Changes in customer demand could make a capital investment unnecessary or stranded in the long term
Security and local political conditions in South Africa could undermine operational improvements if not addressed in parallel
next_steps: Quantify the NPV of each proposed solution (storage facility, fleet upgrade, additional trucks, leasing) against the baseline of current operations
Assess whether shipping volume from other, better-performing plants is a viable short-term alternative while improvements are implemented at this location
Present a final recommendation to senior management with full investment justification to address potential resistance to capital spending
